extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent practitioners drafting/litigating life-sciences claims)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for applying the subject-matter eligibility framework (Step 1; Step 2A/2B) to life-sciences claims, including how to interpret claim terms (BRI), identify judicial exceptions, compare nature-based products to natural counterparts, and evaluate whether additional elements provide 'significantly more.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory category (Step 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim is directed to a statutory category of invention (process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim recites a process (a series of steps/acts), a manufacture, a composition of matter, etc., Step 1 is satisfied (e.g., process = series of steps such as 'obtaining a plasma sample' and 'detecting JUL-1').

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify judicial exception(s)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim is directed to any judicial exception: laws of nature, natural phenomena/product of nature, or abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a claimed correlation between a biomarker and disease can be a law of nature; mental comparison/critical thinking steps can be an abstract idea; isolated or unmodified natural products can be a 'product of nature' exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI) of claim terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpret claim language under the broadest reasonable interpretation when evaluating eligibility (e.g., 'cream', 'vaccine', 'immuno-effective amount', 'microneedle array').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the plain meaning in the relevant art to identify embodiments encompassed by the claim (e.g., 'cream' = semi-solid homogeneous emulsion comprising water and oil; 'vaccine' = mixture of peptide and adjuvant sufficient to produce immunogenic response). BRI informs which embodiments/counterparts to compare in the exception analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-of-nature: compare to closest naturally occurring counterpart
rubrics_metrics.description: For nature-based products, compare the claimed subject matter to its closest naturally occurring counterpart to determine if it has 'markedly different characteristics.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If components do not occur together in nature, compare the claimed mixture to its individual natural components. If a component occurs naturally in combination with others, use that combination as the closest counterpart. The analysis asks whether the claimed item exhibits marked differences relative to that counterpart.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markedly different characteristics — structural/physical/functional
rubrics_metrics.description: Marked differences can be in structural, physical, functional, or other characteristics; such differences can show the claim is not a 'product of nature.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete examples: structural/physical — emulsification producing small uniform oil droplets homogeneously dispersed in water causing a semi-solid, non-flowable cream that adheres to skin; functional — a mixture exhibiting greatly enhanced immunogenicity (e.g., 30% + 0% -> 80% seroprotection). Even functional changes (increased immunogenicity) can constitute 'marked differences.'

rubrics_metrics.name: When no naturally occurring mixture exists, compare to natural components
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claimed combination of substances does not occur together in nature, compare the claimed mixture to the natural components individually.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: peptide + aluminum phosphate + water — because the three do not occur together, compare to peptide and to the water/aluminum-phosphate counterpart (if that combination occurs naturally), and evaluate marked differences accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process claims focused on action vs. product limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim as a whole is focused on a process (e.g., detecting a protein), the existence of nature-based product limitations in the claim does not always require performing the 'markedly different characteristics' analysis on those product limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a detection method that recites a plasma sample and JUL-1 may be analyzed as a process, and the eligibility inquiry can end at Step 2A when the claim is not directed to an exception as a whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A / Step 2B: 'significantly more' / additional elements analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim is directed to a judicial exception, determine whether elements beyond the exception — individually or in combination — amount to 'significantly more' such that the claim is a patent-eligible application of the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether additional elements are meaningful limitations that confine the exception to a particular useful application (not merely instructions to 'apply' the exception). Consider whether the limitation is unconventional and whether the combination yields an improvement in a technical field (analogous to Diehr).

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-understood, routine, conventional activities do not confer eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements that are well-understood, routine, and conventional at the time of filing — especially when recited at a high level of generality — do not add 'significantly more.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: obtaining a sample, using generic detection techniques, or adding routine data-gathering steps are insufficient. The guidance stresses that mere physical/tangible nature of additional elements (e.g., obtaining a sample) does not automatically confer eligibility (citing Alice/Diehr principles).

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination of conventional elements may still be insufficient unless it improves the technical field
rubrics_metrics.description: Consideration of elements as a combination can add 'significantly more' only if the combination provides a meaningful, technical improvement beyond conventional practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with Diehr where elements taken together improved a technical process; here, if the elements only bring conventional activities together without providing a new technical solution, they fail to transform an exception into eligible subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unconventional, specific limitations can provide 'significantly more'
rubrics_metrics.description: Recitation of specific, unconventional reagents, treatments, or devices that were not routine or conventional at the time of filing can render a claim eligible by supplying 'significantly more.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited: detecting JUL-1 using a porcine anti-JUL-1 antibody (not conventionally used for human proteins), detecting using a specific monoclonal antibody mAb-D33, administering topical vitamin D (not previously routine for julitis), and a coated microneedle array as an unconventional delivery device. Such limitations can confine the claim to a particular useful application and thereby amount to 'significantly more' (Step 2B yes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and explain exception and insufficiency in Office actions (practice note)
rubrics_metrics.description: When issuing rejections or reasons for allowance, the examiner should identify the claim limitation that is an exception and explain why it is an exception and why additional elements do or do not amount to 'significantly more.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A rejection should point to the claim element (e.g., a correlation step) and explain that it is a law of nature/abstract idea/product of nature, and then explain why the other claim limitations are merely data-gathering or well-understood, routine and conventional activities (or why they are unconventional and therefore sufficient). Remarks may also be added when a claim is allowed to clarify that it 'is not directed to any judicial exception.'
